Reading · the small thing that changed everything

1.1 Discuss. Has anything good ever happened to you completely by chance? What was it?

KEY WORDS

serendipity finding something good by chance

random with no plan or pattern

to subscribe to pay regularly for a service

a chance a possibility; an opportunity

The Small Thing That Changed Everything

Ask people how their life took the shape it has, and almost nobody describes a decision. They describe an accident — usually a very small one.

TOM, 38. I missed a train. That's the whole story. I was going to a conference in Manchester and I got to the platform four minutes late, so I sat in the station café for an hour and a half. A woman asked if she could share my table because the place was full. We talked about nothing. Eleven years later she is still asking me to pass things at breakfast. If I'd caught that train I would have gone to the conference, learned nothing, and come home.

BETTY, 54. Somebody gave me the wrong parcel. It was a book about beekeeping and it was meant for a neighbour three doors down, but the handwriting on the label was terrible and it came to me. I read forty pages before I realised. I have eleven hives now. I still don't know who the neighbour was, and I have never given the book back.

CARLA, 29. I subscribed to the wrong newsletter — I wanted one about film and I clicked the one below it, which was about grants for small businesses. I nearly unsubscribed twice. Six months later it listed a grant that exactly fitted an idea my sister and I had been talking about for years, and we applied on the last possible day. If I'd been more organised about my inbox, none of this would have happened.

2

Grammar · the third conditional

PRESENTATION

In 10A you used the second conditional for an unreal present. The third conditional does the same job for an unreal past — and the past cannot be changed, so every third conditional is about something that did not happen.

2nd Unreal present. If I had more money, I would buy a flat. — I don't have it, but I might one day.

3rd Unreal past. If I'd caught that train, I would have gone to the conference. — I didn't catch it. It is finished. Nothing can change it.

= The formula: If + past perfect, would have + past participle. Two halves, and each half has its own tense. Getting one right and the other wrong is the normal mistake.

↔ Either half can come first. If I'd known, I would have told you. = I would have told you if I'd known. Put the comma in only when the if half comes first.

How to read one backwards. Every third conditional tells you what really happened, in reverse. If I hadn't read her letters, I wouldn't have discovered the truth means: I read them, and I discovered it. Flip both halves to the opposite and you have the facts.

The IF half

The WOULD half

ERROR WARNING

1 The IF half is past perfect, not present perfect. ✗ If you have been there… → ✓ If you had been there…

2 The other half needs WOULD HAVE, not the past perfect. ✗ It had been better to stay at home. → ✓ It would have been better to stay at home. This is the commonest error at B1+.

3 And not WOULD or WILL alone. ✗ If I'd known, I would tell you. → ✓ I would have told you. ✗ …I will tell you. → the past is closed; will cannot go there.

4 HAVE is not HAD, and HAD is not HAVE. ✗ if he'd have more time → ✓ if he'd had more time. ✗ could burned → ✓ could have burned.

5 Question word order. ✗ What you would have done? → ✓ What would you have done? The would jumps in front of the subject, exactly as in any question.

PRONUNCIATION

The H in HAVE disappears completely. would have → /wʊdəv/ · wouldn't have → /wʊdntəv/ · could have → /kʊdəv/. The final consonant of would links straight onto a weak /əv/.

Which is why students write OF. would of gone is a spelling of what they hear, and it is wrong. Hear /əv/, write have — always.

Vocabulary · do, make and take

PRESENTATION

Three verbs that mean almost nothing on their own. The noun decides which one you need, and there is no rule that always works — but there is one that works often.

DO — a longer activity, usually work. do a job · do some research · do a hobby · do your best · do voluntary work · do somebody a favour

MAKE — you create something that wasn't there. make money · make a decision · make friends · make a mistake · make the most of something · make your own luck

TAKE — a quick action or decision. take a photo · take a look · take a chance · take an opportunity · take somebody's advice · take a break

The one worth memorising: you make the most of an opportunity, and you take the opportunity itself. Both appear in this unit, two lines apart, and students swap them constantly.

PRONUNCIATION — WHERE THE STRESS FALLS

In all of these, the noun is the loud word and the verb is almost thrown away. That is the opposite of what students do.

make a deCISion · take a CHANCE · do some reSEARCH · make the MOST of it · take an opporTUNity

Why it matters. If you stress the verb — MAKE a decision — an English listener hears a contrast and waits for you to say what you did not do. Stress the noun and the phrase sounds like one word, which is what it is.

WHY YOU DIDN'T HEAR IT

A third conditional has six or seven words and only two loud ones. I would have won easily if I hadn't hurt my arm → the stress is on easily and arm. Everything else is squeezed.

So listen for the two nouns at the ends. Each half of the sentence lands on its own loud word, and those two words are the whole meaning. bought… bad condition · pushed… car… hit · truth… letters.

5.2 Greg uses one third conditional. Find it. What is he claiming?

ADVISING A COURSE OF ACTION

English has two kinds of advice phrase, and the difference is not politeness — it is how much of the future you paint.

Advice only: I think you should go for it. · If I were you, I'd write and ask. · Maybe it would be better to… · I'm just suggesting that you look at the alternatives.

Advice plus a picture of what would happen: I think you'd meet a lot of interesting people. · I'm not sure it would be very interesting. · You'd probably regret it.

The second kind is far more persuasive, because it does the imagining for the reader. But it is also a prediction, so only use it where you would be willing to be wrong.

And adverbs set the temperature. definitely · probably · certainly make you sound sure. perhaps · maybe · possibly make you sound careful. Choose before you write, and stay consistent — an email that swings between them sounds like two people.

5.5 Read the two replies. Then answer.

REPLY A

Hi Grace — I think you should definitely go for it. You'd meet people you'd never meet otherwise, and you'd come back with something nobody can take off you. The money is a problem, obviously, but it's a solvable one: ask two local businesses to sponsor you and put the rest on a small loan. I did something similar at your age and it's certainly the best decision I ever made.

REPLY B

Hi Grace — before you decide, I'd maybe look at this from the other side. I'm not sure the elephant programme would be as useful as it sounds; possibly ask them exactly what volunteers do all day. If I were you, I'd also find out where the money goes. I'm just suggesting that you check — it might still be the right thing, but you'd want to know first.
